analysis.one_liner: Taxes big companies whose CEO earns more than 50 times their median worker's pay.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the Senate Finance Committee until Congress ended, with no action after its referral on November 1, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would impose a federal excise tax on large corporations—those with at least $100 million in annual gross receipts and $10 million in annual payroll—when their CEO's pay is more than 50 times the median worker's pay. The tax scales with how far the pay ratio exceeds 50 to 1, capped at 1% of the company's gross receipts. Its purpose is to give corporations a financial reason to shrink CEO pay packages or raise worker wages.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at very large companies whose CEO pay is more than 50 times the median wage. The tax pressure gives their employer a financial reason to raise median wages or rein in executive compensation. It also benefits the general public through revenue and by discouraging extreme pay inequality.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers at big corporations with extreme CEO pay

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an excise tax on employers with at least $100 million in gross receipts and $10 million in payroll when the CEO-to-median-worker pay ratio exceeds 50 to 1.
The tax is capped at 1% of the employer's gross receipts, limiting the maximum financial hit.
For the first time, stock awards and elective deferrals are counted alongside wages in computing executive compensation for the ratio.
The bill directs regulations to prevent companies from gaming the ratio by replacing employees with contractors.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations—those with at least $100 million in gross receipts and $10 million in payroll—whose CEO pay exceeds 50 times the median worker's pay. They would either pay the tax or change their pay practices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Very large corporations with high CEO pay

drawbacks.text: The tax applies only to the largest companies, so mid-size firms with extreme pay ratios face no tax pressure at all.
Because the tax is capped at 1% of gross receipts, for the biggest companies the maximum penalty may be too small relative to profits to change executive pay behavior.
Business groups generally oppose pay-ratio taxes as an inappropriate use of the tax code to dictate private compensation decisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's goal—narrowing the gap between CEO and worker pay at the largest companies—would benefit ordinary workers, though the 1%-of-gross-receipts cap limits how hard the tax actually bites, so its practical effect on pay practices is uncertain.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on November 1, 2023, and never received any further action—no hearing, no markup, no floor vote—before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 1, 2023, by Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse with Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Jeff Merkley.
On the same day it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
No further action was taken on the bill for the remainder of the 118th Congress, which ended January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations with extreme CEO-to-worker pay gaps are better off, since the tax never became law and their compensation structures remain untouched. The Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on the bill, also avoided taking a position on the issue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High pay-ratio corporations that avoid the tax

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on November 1, 2023, and took no further action—no hearing, no markup, no vote—for the rest of the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's three sponsors were all Democrats; no Republican cosponsored it, and the bill never advanced out of committee for a floor vote.

industries.industry: Very large corporations with high CEO pay
industries.note: These firms would face a new excise tax if their CEO earns more than 50 times their median worker's pay. The tax never became law, so their compensation structures remain untouched.

industries.industry: Executive compensation consultants and law firms
industries.note: These firms advise corporations on pay structures that would have needed restructuring under the bill's ratio test; since the bill died, their services remain in demand under the status quo.
